seo_title: Bunny Man: the 1970 Virginia attacks and Bunny Man Bridge
seo_desc: The Bunny Man started as two real police reports in Fairfax County in October 1970. Here is what happened on Guinea Road, how the legend grew, and what to know before you visit Bunny Man Bridge.
summary: A man in a rabbit suit with an axe, chased back to two police reports from Burke, Virginia in October 1970 and then buried under fifty years of invented murders.
body: The Bunny Man is a northern Virginia legend about a figure in a rabbit costume who threatens people with an axe, usually at the Colchester Overpass near Clifton, which everyone now calls Bunny Man Bridge.

This one has a documented start, which is unusual. Fairfax County Public Library historian Brian Conley traced it to two police reports from Burke in October 1970, ten days apart. A man in a bunny suit threw a hatchet through a parked car's window in the first one, and a man in a bunny costume chopped at a porch post and threatened a security guard in the second.

Everything after that is embellishment. The escaped asylum inmate, the murders, the bodies under the bridge, the dead rabbits hanging from the rail, none of it is in the police record, and a 1973 university paper found the story already had 54 versions.

sections.h: Guinea Road, just after midnight, October 19, 1970
p: Robert Bennett was a cadet at the US Air Force Academy, home visiting relatives on Guinea Road in Burke with his fiancée. They were coming back from a football game and parked in a field around midnight to walk over to an uncle's house across the road, engine still running.

Something moved outside the back window. Then a man in a white suit with long rabbit ears ran out of the bushes shouting that they were on private property and that he had their tag number. He threw a hatchet through the passenger window and ran off. Bennett and his fiancée got out of there, and the hatchet was still on the floorboard when they got to the police.

There's a wrinkle in this one that I like, because it's how real reports read. Bennett said the man had long bunny ears. His fiancée said there were no ears, just a white pointed hood of some kind. Both of them got a clear look at his face but couldn't tell his race in the dark. The police examined the hatchet, found nothing to work with, and gave it back to Bennett. The case closed.

sections.h: Ten days later, Kings Park West
p: On the evening of October 31, 1970, a construction security guard named Paul Phillips walked up to a man standing on the porch of an unfinished empty house in Kings Park West, off the same road. Phillips said the man was wearing a grey, black and white bunny costume, looked about 20, 5 ft 8 and around 175 lb.

Phillips tried to talk to him and the man started chopping at a porch post with a long-handled axe. Some accounts count eight gashes in the post. He told Phillips that all you people trespass around here, and that if Phillips came any closer he'd chop his head off.

Phillips went back to his car for his handgun. By the time he got back the rabbit was gone into the woods. That was the last documented sighting of a man in a rabbit suit with an axe, and it's the one that started the whole thing.

sections.h: The month it became a story
p: Once the Washington Post got hold of it, the calls came in. More than 50 people contacted police saying they'd seen the Bunny Man. One newspaper story said he'd eaten somebody's runaway cat. People rang the detective handling the case, W.L. Johnson of the Criminal Investigation Bureau, with tips and sightings, and most of it was prank calls and schoolyard rumour.

One call was different. A construction worker in the subdivision said someone had phoned him calling himself the Axe Man and complained about people dumping stumps, limbs and brush on his property, and asked him to meet that night to sort it out. Police staked the place out. Nobody showed.

That phone call is the closest thing to a motive in the whole case, and it points at something dull and believable. A local man with a grudge about trespassing and dumping, in a half-built subdivision, using a costume to scare people off.

sections.h: How a guy with a hatchet became a murderer
p: In 1973 a University of Maryland student named Patricia Johnson wrote a research paper that logged exactly 54 versions of the two incidents. The plot held, but the details drifted all over the place, and a handful of versions already had the Bunny Man killing people, which the police record never did.

The version that took over the internet came later. In 1999 somebody posting as Timothy J. Forbes on a site called Castle of Spirits wrote that the Bunny Man was a convict named Douglas J. Grifon who escaped from a bus in 1904 and butchered people at the bridge for decades. Conley checked it and found the specifics are false, every one. The murders never happened, and the Old Clifton Library the writer claimed as a source never existed.
That's the whole mystery solved, if you ask me. Two odd nights in 1970, one very good newspaper story, and then fifty years of people adding gore because it makes a better campfire story.

The Colchester Overpass is a narrow one-lane railroad bridge over Colchester Road near Clifton, built around 1906 near the old Sangster's Station. It's on a working rail line, so the tracks on top are live and the land around them isn't yours to wander.

Because of the legend, the bridge became a place to go at night, and it's covered in graffiti from decades of visitors. Fairfax County started controlling access around Halloween back in 2003. Over Halloween in 2011, more than 200 people, some from as far as the Pennsylvania line, were turned away at a 14-hour checkpoint.

So yes, you can drive under it and have a look, and people do it every week. What you shouldn't do is climb the embankment, walk the tracks or hang around after dark, because the danger at Bunny Man Bridge has never been a rabbit. It's trains and trespassing charges.

faq.a: Two incidents are documented. In October 1970 a man in a rabbit outfit threw a hatchet through a car window in Burke, Virginia, and a man in a bunny costume chopped at a porch post and threatened a security guard nearby. Fairfax County library historian Brian Conley found no record of any killings, and the escaped inmate story that everyone repeats is a 1999 internet invention.

faq.q: Is the Bunny Man still alive?
faq.a: Nobody knows who he was, so there's no way to say. If he was the roughly 20-year-old the security guard described in 1970, he'd be in his mid seventies now. There hasn't been a documented attack since October 1970, only the story getting bigger.

faq.q: Can you visit Bunny Man Bridge?
faq.a: You can drive under it on Colchester Road near Clifton, Virginia, and that's the sensible way to see it. The overpass carries an active railroad line, so don't climb up or walk the tracks. Police watch the area around Halloween and have turned away hundreds of people at checkpoints.

faq.q: Why does the Bunny Man have an axe?
faq.a: Because that's what both 1970 reports describe. A hatchet came through a car window in the first one and a long-handled axe was used on a porch post in the second. The later versions turned the axe into something supernatural, but the original weapon was just a tool a local guy probably had in his truck.

faq.q: Where did the story of the asylum escape come from?
faq.a: A 1999 post on a website called Castle of Spirits, written by somebody using the name Timothy J. Forbes. It named the Bunny Man as Douglas J. Grifon, an inmate who escaped in 1904 and killed people at the bridge. Conley checked every detail and found all of it false, including the library the author cited as a source. It never existed.

faq.q: What is the Bunny Man's real name?
faq.a: It was never established. The only name that shows up, Douglas J. Grifon, came out of a fictional 1999 internet post. Police in 1970 had no suspect, and the case closed without one.
